subject: 20260913-191409-sweep-deepgram-30
headline: The agent handled 40 calls at once without slowing down, but callers wait longest after saying thanks at the end, and calls where it mishears them are the ones that fail the refund task.

insights.title: The closing turn is slow because of the reply step, and slower still when the agent hears only part of the caller
evidence: calls log, turn 4: most_common_reply "You're welcome! Your refund will be processed shortly."
insights.finding: The wait before the agent speaks has three parts: the network round trip, endpointing (the agent noticing the caller has stopped) and think_speak (the agent working out its reply and starting to say it). On the closing turn, endpointing is the fastest of any turn, so hearing the caller is not what slows it. The time goes into think_speak. On this turn, 24 transcripts held under half of the caller's words. Those turns waited longer at the median than turns heard in full. Yet even turns heard in full are far slower here than on earlier turns. So two things add up on this turn. The reply step is slow on every call, and cutting the caller short makes it worse. One possibility is that the agent does refund work at this point, since its usual reply confirms the refund. Another is that the quicker endpointing ends the caller's turn before they finish. The data does not show either.
insights.why_it_matters: This one turn is where long silences come from. A caller who hears nothing after saying thanks may hang up before the refund is confirmed.
insights.next_step: Trace the reply step on turn 4 for a sample of calls, including any tool or refund calls and the model request. Read the 24 cut-short transcripts next to the caller's line to see where the agent stopped listening.

insights.title: Two scripted checks fail on every call while the step verdicts say pass
evidence: c40: nodes open pass_rate 0.0% (checked 80), miss said none of ["reference reply"]
c40: nodes number pass_rate 0.0% (checked 80), miss said none of ["reference reply"]
c40: nodes close checked 0 of visits 80
c40: quality verdict pass, compared includes the open check and the number check
judge: criterion 'asks the user for an order number before discussing the order' missed 0 of judged 210
calls log, turn 1: most_common_reply "I can help with that. Can you provide your order number, please?"
insights.finding: The open and number checks score 0.0% in every step. Each miss reads 'said none of ["reference reply"]', which looks like a placeholder phrase rather than something the agent would say. The close check graded no calls. The judge (an AI model that grades whole calls) found the agent asked for the order number on every judged call, and the usual first reply does ask for it. The step quality verdict still reads pass, even though it lists these checks among the things it compared.
insights.why_it_matters: When checks can never pass, the verdict stops meaning anything. A real failure on the opening or order-number turn would go unnoticed.
insights.next_step: Replace the "reference reply" placeholder in the open and number checks with the phrases the agent should say, and add a check for the close node. Then confirm the quality verdict fails when a check scores zero.

insights.title: Calls where the agent mishears the caller are the ones that fail the refund task
evidence: judge correlation: misheard_pass_rate 86.4% (44 calls), conclusive true
judge: criterion 'confirms a refund after the user asks for their money back' missed 6 of 210
insights.finding: Word error rate (WER) is the share of the caller's words the agent's transcript got wrong or dropped. The judge graded all 210 calls. Every call below the 5.0% mishearing threshold did the job. Among calls above it, the pass rate fell to 86.4%. Failed calls had a much higher median WER than calls that passed. All the misses are on one criterion: confirming the refund after the caller asks for their money back. In the judge's example, the agent asked for confirmation again instead of confirming.
insights.why_it_matters: Task failures here seem to come from hearing errors, not from load or speed. Faster replies alone will not fix them.
insights.next_step: Pull the 6 calls that missed the refund criterion and compare what the caller said with the agent's transcript on the refund request.

insights.title: Latency holds flat from 20 to 40 calls, but the slowest waits sit above Coval's load line
insights.finding: p50 is the typical wait and p95 is the wait that only the slowest 5 in 100 turns exceed. Both barely move from 20 to 40 calls at once, and the c40 step stayed steady from its first half to its second. So the agent showed no sign of reaching its limit at 40 calls. At c40, the typical wait is under Hamming's observed production median, but p95 is above Coval's published 2000ms load target. Both are other teams' lines, not this team's targets. The baseline, c5 and c10 steps measured a struggling test machine, not the agent, so they cannot serve as a clean starting point. The comparison rests on c20 and c40 only.
insights.why_it_matters: More simultaneous calls is not the risk at this size. The slow tail exists at every valid load, so fixing it means changing the agent, not adding capacity.
insights.next_step: Rerun the low-load steps on a test machine that keeps up, then extend the sweep past 40 calls at once to find where latency starts to rise.
